title: 600 KB WebGL shooter made with the $20 Claude Code plan in a month (Opus 4.6)
author: c35683
selftext:
A little contrast to all the Fable/Astra posts. Say hello to, uh... Quank?

**Some important details:**

* The game is 100% javascript+WebGL, which means it acts as its own source code, and runs entirely on the front end
* It's more polished than the footage shows at this point, but I wanted to show a version done over around a month in total (with breaks)
* It uses a sector system similar to Doom or Duke Nukem 3d, which heavily optimizes rendering geometry and allows for features like mirrors and non-Euclidean levels
* The 600 KB size applies to a minified version, otherwise it's around 2 MB
* **I'm planning on open sourcing the game and the level editor once it's done**

**What's vibe-coded:**

* Most of the game, including the sector-based rendering engine (although some parts are based on very specific instructions)
* Enemy models, rigging and animations (with small manual edits)
* The level editor and model visualizer

**What's done manually:**

* Parameter and flag tweaks (e.g. physics values, enemy speed, explosion sizes, etc.)
* Surface textures (although they're heavily based on procedural AI-generated ones)
* Level design, although the editor is vibe-coded, so only features it supports are allowed

**Workflow:**

My workflow admittedly wasn't anything fancy (for example, I didn't find any use for skills other than headless testing), as it was my first vibe-coded project to learn Claude Code.

The project started out and was mostly done in Opus 4.6, splitting features into chunks which could be handled in between Claude's 5-hour naps. I settled on creating an internal git-ignored directory with 'to do' files in .md format, usually going into details about how the algorithms for features (like the sector system) should work, and pointing Claude Code to whatever task needed to be done in plan mode, then negotiating the result if necessary and either keeping it or rolling things back and doing them another way.

I moved over to Opus 4.8 recently and it's slightly cheaper, and much better at agentic coding and testing, but also has an annoying habit of burying code under a mountain of comments.

The things AI struggled the most with was sector geometry (floating point errors, etc.) and drawing functions for the level editor. On the other hand, it turned out to be surprisingly good at rigging and animating models.

As a side note, vibe-coding and optimizing a 3d rendering engine from scratch and dealing with all the floating point and geometry errors has seriously raised my respect for the 90's id Software folk behind Doom and Quake (including the interdimensional time-travelling space wizard genius and actual rocket scientist John Carmack).

*The music is remixed from SubspaceAudio's 400 Indie Game Music Loops collection, which I bought.*

replies.body:
One easy implementation for this  could be a charge station to replenish  your armor level with a unit mounted on the wall just like half-life did back in the old days, but with your own style & design. 
Perhaps small rooms/laboratories scattered throughout the maps? Idk what will fit your story but you get the idea 😅

replies.author: c35683
replies.body:
Not a bad idea, but it doesn't really fit the 1994-1996 Doom/Quake/BUILD Engine era I was aiming for.

The original inspiration was Quake, which famously had no "use" key so you wouldn't be distracted from the combat loop and all buttons were pressed either by walking into or shooting them. Some things I want to do though are more environmental details, like torches or furniture, animated water/lava, more textures, and more map details. And maybe destructible terrain.
